planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to a shaded location March-May. Freddie needs a large pot and room to spread, since its leaves become some of the biggest in the rhizomatous group.

directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist but never waterlogged soil, and give it the largest pot of any rhizomatous begonia in the collection. Freddie is prized for producing some of the largest leaves in the rhizomatous group, with mature specimens capable of leaves well over a foot across under good conditions, each one asymmetrical, deeply veined, and marked in rich combinations of green and silver along the vein lines. The thick, creeping rhizome spreads steadily across the pot surface and benefits from being allowed to climb slightly over the rim rather than being buried. Water at the soil level to avoid leaf spot, let the top inch of soil dry between waterings, and propagate by rhizome division once the clump outgrows its container.
sources: American Begonia Society — Rhizomatous Begonia Variety Classification

common_name: Bessie Buxton Begonia (Upright Pond-Lily Rhizomatous Begonia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to a shaded location March-May. Bessie Buxton performs best as a container plant brought indoors when temperatures drop below 55°F.

directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist but never waterlogged soil. Bessie Buxton is a long-cultivated rhizomatous begonia named for an early leader of the American Begonia Society, grown for its glossy, rounded, dark green leaves carried on an upright rather than trailing rhizome, giving it a tidier, more vertical habit than many sprawling rhizomatous types. The thick, almost succulent leaf stalks and compact clumping growth make it well suited to a standard pot rather than a hanging basket. Water at the soil level to avoid leaf spot, let the top inch of soil dry between waterings, and propagate by rhizome division or leaf cuttings.
sources: American Begonia Society — Bessie Buxton biography and cultivar notes

common_name: Black Velvet Begonia (Near-Black Velvety Rhizomatous Begonia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to a shaded location March-May. Black Velvet performs best as a container plant brought indoors when temperatures drop below 55°F.

directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist but never waterlogged soil, since the darkest leaf color develops away from strong direct sun. Black Velvet, also sold as Hocking Black Velvet, carries rounded, deeply saturated near-black leaves with a soft matte, velvety texture that reads almost purple-black in low light and takes on a faint olive cast in brighter conditions. Its compact, clumping rhizome and relatively slow growth make it a good fit for smaller pots and mixed shade containers where a strong dark color accent is wanted against brighter foliage. Water at the soil level to avoid leaf spot, let the top inch of soil dry between waterings, and propagate by rhizome division.

common_name: Joe Hayden Begonia (Mahogany Star-Leaf Rhizomatous Begonia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to a shaded location March-May. Joe Hayden performs best as a container plant brought indoors when temperatures drop below 55°F.

directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist but never waterlogged soil. Joe Hayden is a long-established rhizomatous hybrid with a very compact, tightly mounding habit and glossy, thick, star-shaped leaves colored in deep mahogany and olive-green on top with ruby-red undersides visible along the edges, a striking two-tone effect not shared by most other rhizomatous types. Its dense, slow-spreading rhizome keeps the plant tidy in a small pot for a long time before it needs dividing. Water at the soil level to avoid leaf spot, let the top inch of soil dry between waterings, and propagate by rhizome division or leaf cuttings.
sources: American Begonia Society — rhizomatous begonia cultivar notes

common_name: Anna Lee Salisbury Begonia (Thick-Leaf Winter-Blooming Rhizomatous Begonia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to a shaded location March-May. Anna Lee Salisbury is a large rhizomatous begonia that benefits from a sizeable pot to reach full bloom size.

directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist but never waterlogged soil. Anna Lee Salisbury grows from an unusually thick rhizome and carries large, thick, dark green leaves marked with light-colored veining, building into a substantial clump over time that is larger than many compact rhizomatous types. It is a winter bloomer, sending up clusters of white flowers from roughly December through March when most other houseplants are dormant, a welcome bit of color during the darkest months. Water at the soil level to avoid leaf spot, let the top inch of soil dry between waterings, and propagate by rhizome division.
sources: American Begonia Society — rhizomatous begonia cultivar notes

common_name: President Carnot Begonia (Heirloom Cane-Type Angel Wing Begonia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to a shaded to partially shaded location March-May, staking the tall cane stems as needed.

directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist but never waterlogged soil, staking the jointed cane stems for support as the plant matures. President Carnot is one of the older named cane-type begonias still in cultivation, with pointed, wing-shaped leaves on tall, bamboo-like canes that form a substantial upright shrub over a season or two, much in the manner of its better-known relative Lucerna. Its long history in collector and heirloom plant circles has kept it in circulation among begonia enthusiasts even as showier modern hybrids have come and gone. Pinch young cane tips to encourage branching and a fuller habit, water at the soil level to avoid leaf spot, and let the top inch of soil dry between waterings.

common_name: Sinbad Begonia (Bronze-Tinted Cane Begonia with Pendant Pink Flowers)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to a shaded to partially shaded location March-May.

directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist but never waterlogged soil. Sinbad is a cane-type hybrid with silvery-green leaves that emerge with a pink-and-bronze tint when young and mature to a soft metallic sheen, a more subtle coloring than the bold silver-spotted angel wing types. Loose, pendant clusters of small pink flowers hang from the upper canes through the warm season, giving the plant a light, airy bloom display rather than the heavy flower clusters of larger cane cultivars. Pinch young cane tips to encourage branching, water at the soil level to avoid leaf spot, and let the top inch of soil dry between waterings.

common_name: My Special Angel Begonia (Compact Silver-Spotted Cane Begonia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to a shaded to partially shaded location March-May. My Special Angel stays more compact than large cane types, suiting smaller pots and windowsills.

directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist but never waterlogged soil. My Special Angel is a compact medium-cane begonia with lustrous green, silver-spotted wing-shaped leaves, staying noticeably smaller and bushier than tall cane heirlooms like Lucerna, which makes it a better fit for windowsills and small containers. It produces plump, rounded clusters of shell-pink flowers over much of the year under good light, a steadier bloom cycle than many seasonal cane types. Pinch young cane tips to encourage branching and a fuller habit, water at the soil level to avoid leaf spot, and let the top inch of soil dry between waterings.

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to a shaded to partially shaded location March-May, staking the tall cane stems as needed.

directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist but never waterlogged soil, staking the jointed cane stems for support as the plant matures. Elaine is a large-leaved cane begonia with speckled foliage and some of the largest flower clusters among angel wing types, producing big, showy umbels of brilliant coral-pink blooms that hang well below the canes. Its vigorous, upright growth builds into a substantial shrubby specimen over a season or two, making it a strong backdrop or focal plant in a shaded bed or large container. Pinch young cane tips to encourage branching, water at the soil level to avoid leaf spot, and let the top inch of soil dry between waterings.

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to a shaded to partially shaded location March-May.

directions: Plant in shade to partial shade in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist but never waterlogged soil. Cotton Candy is a cane-type begonia grown for its abundant clusters of soft pink flowers set against medium green, lightly spotted wing-shaped leaves, blooming over a long stretch of the warm season. Its moderate, multi-caned growth habit is easier to keep tidy in a standard container than the largest tree-like cane cultivars, while still giving the classic angel wing look. Pinch young cane tips to encourage branching, water at the soil level to avoid leaf spot, and let the top inch of soil dry between waterings.

common_name: Pollux Rex Begonia (Stippled-Leaf Jointed Rex Begonia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to a shaded location March-May. Pollux performs best as a container plant brought indoors when temperatures drop below 55°F.

directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist but never waterlogged soil. Pollux is a Rex-type begonia distinguished from many other rex cultivars by stems that are visibly jointed at or just below the soil line, giving the base of the plant a segmented, almost bamboo-like look before the leaves take over. Its rounded leaves carry a fine stippled texture across the metallic surface, adding a speckled dimension to the typical rex sheen. As with other rex begonias, small flowers are secondary to the foliage display and are often removed. Water at the soil level to avoid leaf spot, let the top inch of soil dry between waterings, and propagate by leaf or rhizome cuttings.
sources: American Begonia Society — Rex Cultorum cultivar notes

common_name: Putzeys Rex Begonia (Historic 19th-Century Species-Form Rex Begonia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to a shaded location March-May. Putzeys performs best as a container plant brought indoors when temperatures drop below 55°F.

directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist but never waterlogged soil. Putzeys is one of the oldest named forms in cultivation descending directly from the original nineteenth-century Begonia rex introductions from Southeast Asia, predating most of the elaborate modern rex-cultorum hybrids by well over a century. Its leaves show the classic metallic silver-and-green zonation of the original wild-collected rex plants rather than the heavily ruffled or spiraled forms bred since, making it a useful reference point for how far rex breeding has come. As with other rex begonias, small flowers are secondary to the foliage display. Water at the soil level to avoid leaf spot, let the top inch of soil dry between waterings, and propagate by leaf or rhizome cuttings.

common_name: Flirty Girl Rex Begonia (Fine-Textured Hybrid Rex Begonia)

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to a shaded location March-May. Flirty Girl performs best as a container plant brought indoors when temperatures drop below 55°F.

directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist but never waterlogged soil. Flirty Girl is a hybrid rex-type begonia bred from a cross between the small, fuzzy-leaved species Begonia acetosella and a named rex cultivar, giving it finer leaf texture and a more compact, filled-in habit than many broad-leaved rex hybrids. Its foliage carries the metallic rex sheen in a smaller, more closely held leaf than typical show-type rex cultivars, making it a good fit for crowded windowsill collections. As with other rex begonias, small flowers are secondary to the foliage display. Water at the soil level to avoid leaf spot, let the top inch of soil dry between waterings, and propagate by leaf or rhizome cuttings.
sources: American Begonia Society — Rex Cultorum cultivar notes

planting.note: Plant transplants after all frost danger has passed; in zone 9 move outdoors to a shaded location March-May. Alafia performs best as a container plant brought indoors when temperatures drop below 55°F.

directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist but never waterlogged soil. Alafia is a widely grown rhizomatous hybrid developed in the 1990s from a cross involving the species-type cultivar 'Cowardly', quickly becoming a popular variety among begonia collectors for its vigorous, adaptable growth and attractive patterned foliage on a spreading rhizome. It forms a dense, low mound that offsets readily, making it easy to divide and share. Water at the soil level to avoid leaf spot and crown rot, let the top inch of soil dry between waterings, and divide the rhizome to propagate or refresh an overgrown clump.
sources: American Begonia Society — rhizomatous begonia cultivar notes
